items.title: Anthropic exposes AI operation that DRC journalists never knew existed

s: Disinformation surrounding DRC-Rwanda relations has weakened the diplomatic and public standing of both countries
Featured image from DRC media, created using screenshots from ACP's YouTube channel
In September 2026, Anthropic, an artificial intelligence (AI) development and research company, exposed a network of fake news sites targeting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The investigation revealed that large-scale, AI-powered disinformation campaigns have emerged at a time of conflict when trust in the news is already at an all-time low and resources are severely limited.
This revelation rang alarm bells for African media watchdogs.
The network coordinated around 70 AI-powered fake news sites and generated at least 318 articles on the eastern DRC conflict, relations with Rwanda, and contested mineral resources.
The operation was highly robust.
On X, coordinated accounts amplified content from the AI-run sites, mimicking legitimate media outlets and rewriting articles for different audiences.
According to Anthropic’s report, the LKM Company, a French advertising agency serving clients with strong interests in the DRC-Rwanda conflict, was behind it all.
They found no evidence of direct government involvement.

When Global Voices approached Hobab Watukalusu, a fact-checker, editor, and head of the training and research department at Soma Média Lab in Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, he shared:
Nous n’avions pas identifié cette opération dans toute son ampleur avant sa révélation.

Cela montre les limites auxquelles nous sommes confrontés face à des campagnes capables de produire, à très grande échelle et dans des délais très courts, des contenus qui peuvent paraître crédibles et s’insérer rapidement dans l’écosystème informationnel.
We hadn’t recognized the full extent of the operation before this revelation.
This highlights our limitations when dealing with campaigns that can rapidly generate large-scale, credible-looking content and quickly gain a foothold in the infoscape.
He added that local journalists on the front lines are struggling to keep up as new technologies make it easier than ever to facilitate massive disinformation campaigns.
DR Congolese fact-checkers face a litany of obstacles in slowing disinformation flows across regions.
Hobab outlines the fundamental constraints:
L'accès encore difficile à l'électricité, à une connexion Internet stable et abordable, ainsi que le coût élevé de la vie constituent des contraintes réelles pour les professionnels de l'information.
Ongoing difficulties in accessing electricity, stable and affordable internet connections, and high living costs pose real-world constraints for journalists.
In the DRC, where journalists are already overwhelmed by covering an active military conflict, analyzing potential industrial-scale, AI-generated content is virtually impossible.
Joël Kaseso, another journalist covering disinformation narratives, told Global Voices:
Des ressources existent, mais la plupart sont payantes.
Ce qui limite notre capacité à tout analyser dans ce contexte tendu où les relations diplomatiques et sécuritaires avec les pays voisins, notamment le Rwanda, ne sont plus au bon fixe.
Although resources exist, most are not free.

Amid this tense environment, where diplomatic and security relations with neighboring countries, particularly Rwanda, are strained, this financial barrier limits our ability to conduct a full analysis.

Kaseso has also identified a simple but critical methodology that most journalists use to navigate this situation: analyzing the author’s intentions, the source’s profile (anonymous accounts versus identifiable influencers), and amplification patterns.
However, this requires time and tools that many newsrooms don’t have.
Détecter qu'un contenu a été généré ou manipulé à l'aide de l'intelligence artificielle ne constitue que la première étape.
Il faut ensuite déterminer si ce contenu est trompeur, identifier sa source, comprendre comment il se diffuse et, surtout, établir dans quel objectif il a été produit.
C'est cette chaîne complète de vérification qui demande du temps, des compétences et des ressources.
Detecting AI-generated or AI-manipulated content is only the first step.
The next steps involve determining whether the content is misleading, identifying its source, understanding how it spreads, and, above all, establishing why it was created in the first place.
This comprehensive verification process requires time, skill, and resources.

items.title: Students air their frustrations anonymously online as emigration tempts many young people in North Macedonia

s: ‘Students don’t have to be members of a political party to create change,’ says founder of online media platform

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Students in North Macedonia are not the happiest group: a 2026 survey suggests that over 76 percent of current students are thinking of emigrating.
The main reasons for this being cited are “quality of life” and “finding employment suitable to professional qualifications.”
However, what if students themselves could change that?
North Macedonia, luckily, has people who decided to take their fate into their own hands and help students achieve a better quality of life, not only for themselves, but for many young people.

At first, Goshe Nikolov, at the time a student himself, founded Instagram-based student media, Studentarija, as an entertainment resource, where students from all over the country shared memes about studies and current events.
This outlet now has over 65,000 subscribers, which is a significant number for a country with 53,000 students.

As he comes to the Zoom interview with Global Voices, Nikolov already has nine years of experience running the most successful student media in the country, and with the help of his team of three, has launched a Digital Student Voice, an online platform that enables students across North Macedonia to anonymously report problems related to higher education and student life.
They were able to do it with the help of the Digital Democracy Initiative grant.
Nikolov has a wide smile and a confident attitude; he answers questions with the clarity that could only be gained by years of hands-on experience.
Global Voices (GV): Could you tell us a little about your student media outlet?
How did it start?
How did you manage to gain so many followers and so much engagement?
Is it only on Instagram?
Goshe Nikolov (GN): Studentarija started in 2017, when I was still a student.
I created it from my room in a student dormitory in Skopje.
At that time, Instagram was becoming increasingly popular among students in North Macedonia, but there was no Macedonian Instagram page specifically for students.
So I decided to create one, and quite spontaneously, in the end it got the name Studentarija, which it still has today.
In the beginning, the idea was very simple.
It was a place where students could share funny and relatable content.
For example, memes, funny videos, everyday posts and situations from student life.
So I could never have imagined that one day it would become what it is today.
Over time, the audience kept growing, and I think that demonstrated that there was a real need for such a space.
At the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2020, I started focusing more on the real problems and challenges faced by students in North Macedonia.
Students started coming to us with questions, asking for information and sharing their problems, because they often could not get the information or support they needed elsewhere.
That was when I really understood that Studentarija could play a much bigger role in the lives of students and young people in our country.
So I think the main reasons young people have stayed with us over the years are our openness, transparency, creativity, consistency and, of course, accessibility.
Students in North Macedonia know that they can come directly to us, that we listen to them, and that Studentarija is genuinely built around their experiences and their needs.
GV: So do you think it will remain only on Instagram, or are you planning to use other platforms for further development?

items.title: Activists push for Pakistan to recognise and support people with albinism

s: Pakistan keeps no data on people with albinism, leaving needs unmet in schools, healthcare, and jobs.
Graph from the 2021 study “ Genetic Causes of Oculocutaneous Albinism in Pakistani Population. ” Sajid et al., Genes 2021, 12(4), 492.
CC BY 4.0 via MDPI.

For Adeel Nasir, 24, who has albinism and lives in Kot Radha Kishan, a town in Kasur district, Punjab Province of Pakistan, school meant constant adjustment to challenges that many people around him did not understand.
Because of low vision, he struggled to read what was written on classroom whiteboards.
Some teachers seated him closer to the board, improved the lighting, and gave him written notes.
But one classroom incident remained painful.
Adeel once asked a teacher what qualifications a fighter pilot needs.
He expected encouragement about his ambition.
Instead, he received a response focused on his eyesight.
“First of all, you should be able to see clearly with your eyes,” Adeel recalled the teacher saying.
His classmates laughed.
Years later, he says people still notice his condition before they recognise his abilities.
“My abilities, my degrees, and my skills were ignored because of my weak eyesight and physical appearance,” he said during an in-person interview with Global Voices.

Adeel’s experience reflects a concern that Malooka-Anne Miti-Drummond, the UN Independent Expert on the enjoyment of human rights by persons with albinism, raised during her June 2026 visit to Pakistan.
She said policies, programmes, and data systems overlook people with albinism.
Albinism is a rare, non-contagious, genetically inherited condition caused by reduced or absent production of melanin, the pigment responsible for colour in the skin, hair, and eyes.
Reduced melanin can result in visual impairment and increased vulnerability to ultraviolet (UV) radiation because melanin provides natural protection against sun damage.
People with albinism are born with the condition; it is not contagious and does not affect their intellectual ability.
Pakistan has no separate national estimate of how many people with albinism live in the country.
The UN notes that country-level data on albinism is scarce worldwide, and many countries collect no official statistics on it.
Available estimates put prevalence at roughly one in 17,000 to 20,000 people in many European and North American populations, and higher in some African communities.
The UN has called for better data collection to understand the challenges people with albinism face.
The absence of a national estimate does not mean that people with albinism are absent in Pakistan.
Researchers have documented albinism among Pakistani families despite the missing estimate.

A study of 94 previously unreported Pakistani families with non-syndromic oculocutaneous albinism found disease-causing variants mainly in the TYR and OCA2 genes, two of the major genetic causes of albinism worldwide.
Genetic studies of affected families cannot establish how many people with albinism live in the country.
For Adeel, the lack of recognition shapes how institutions treat his needs.

After a long effort, he obtained a disability certificate, but as he explained, “The disability certificate we received is also issued on the basis of our weak eyesight, not because of albinism itself.”
“There is no place in any office or government institution where a separate form or category under the name of ‘albino’ exists where we can register ourselves,” Adeel added.
The difficulty of documenting albinism ties to a broader gap in disability data.
Many national systems measure disability through functional difficulties and do not record each medical condition separately.
Pakistan’s 2023 Population and Housing Census asked about difficulty seeing, hearing, walking, communicating, remembering, and caring for oneself rather than individual conditions.
A Pakistan Bureau of Statistics representative, who spoke to Global Voices on condition of anonymity, said the bureau keeps no separate official data on people with albinism.
The person said collecting information on rare conditions requires well-designed questionnaires, and Pakistan would have to choose the best method before adding albinism to future data collection.

items.title: At the UN, plans for a global coalition to attack LGBTQ+ and reproductive rights

s: Far-right activists are trying to dismantle global protections for LGBTQ+ people under the guise of ‘family values’
US President Trump speaking at the U.N.
General Assembly.
Photo by The White House. Fair use.
This article by Hope Pisoni was originally published by Uncloseted Media, an LGBTQ+ focused investigative news outlet, on October 1, 2026.
An edited version is being republished on Global Voices as part of a content partnership agreement.
It has been edited for length and style.

On September 17, while the United Nations (U.N.) was hosting its annual General Assembly for diplomats and leaders from all over the world, several key figures filled a room across the street at the Millennium Hilton in Midtown Manhattan.
Attendees included Trump administration officials, leaders of anti-LGBTQ+ hate groups, far-right politicians from Latin America and reporters from far-right media.

These people were meeting for the Global Forum for Life, Family and Freedoms, a two-day summit of right-wing leaders with an ambitious goal to create a new “pro-life and pro-family” Core Group at the U.N.
Since 2008, the U.N. has had an LGBTI Core Group with 42 member states whose mission is to advocate for LGBTQ+ rights on a global stage.
But the organizers of this new group hope to create an opposing organization to push for policies that undermine reproductive and LGBTQ+ rights around the globe.

Aarón Lara, the Mexico-based conservative activist who came up with the idea for the group, said in an August article that the existing LGBTI Core Group has only been successful because there has not been organized conservative opposition, which a new core group would provide.
Lara (left) speaking with a reporter in the Dominican Republic in March.
Screenshot via Central Noticias YouTube.

“[The LGBTI Core Group] has successfully established victimhood narratives and incorporated observances with global impact. … I always use this example: If it were a soccer match and one team failed to show up, the winner by default would be the team that was present,” Lara said.
Lara and other supporters of the group agreed at the forum to draw up plans for its creation in the coming months.

They may be encouraged to move quickly because the group’s leaders have said they want to use the U.S.’s global influence and capitalize on the current administration’s anti-LGBTQ and anti-abortion stance to do it.
The U.S. recently left the LGBTI Core Group, an early move by Trump in his second term.
The LGBTI Core Group describes itself as “an informal cross-regional group of United Nations Member States.

While it is not an official U.N. body, its work includes ensuring that LGBTQ+ people are considered and protected across all of the U.N.’s activities, from humanitarian aid to human rights resolutions.
For example, one of the first U.N. resolutions to reference LGBTQ+ people was one protecting civilians against extrajudicial executions.
When some members tried to remove LGBTQ people from those protections, advocates and allies fought to keep them in place.

Maria Sjödin, executive director of Outright International, an NGO that focuses on supporting LGBTQ rights worldwide, told Uncloseted Media that work like this could be in jeopardy should the new core group come to fruition.

“We’re talking about the protection of some very basic human rights, and that the opposition to that is trying to organize to make it even more difficult to pass such a thing is really quite horrible,” she says.
Core groups are not official U.N. bodies, so there is no strictly required procedure for their creation.

While there have been other core groups established at the U.N., the LGBTI group is unique in that it is designed for continuous operation on multiple issues rather than as a response to a specific conflict or crisis.
The “pro-life, pro-family” core group would change that, threatening to shift the balance of power at the U.N.

items.title: How an extremist network articulated a hoax linking Brazil’s President Lula to child abuse on X

s: Monitoring of 1,819 posts showed far-right users tried to manipulate Grok, X’s AI tool
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Art by: Méuri Elle/Aos Fatos, used with permission.

A few days before the first round of the 2026 general elections in Brazil on October 4, it took only a few hours for a line said by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about preventive exams for prostate cancer to be twisted into a pedophilia accusation against him.
Aos Fatos obtained and checked 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter), which reconstructed how this hoax was planted and harvested by Bolsonarista users on social media between September 28 and 29.

The distortion in the meaning of Lula’s speech stemmed from a false pedophilia accusation that had already been boosted hours ahead of a statement he made at a campaign event in the city of Belém, Pará state, on September 28.
Users manipulated questions asked to Grok, X’s AI assistance tool, to make it state “Lula consumes CP” — an acronym in English for child pornography.
The chatbot warned that the sentence was wordplay and that it had no records to support the claim.
However, the edit cut from Lula’s speech, shared on social media, gave the narrative new momentum.

Besides requests to make the video viral and to mobilize influencers, some publications also revived old episodes and characters without any connection to Lula’s line to back theories associating the president with child abuse.

During his rally, Lula was talking about the importance of cancer prevention and criticizing men’s resistance to having prostate exams, compared to women’s healthcare culture, which, according to him, is used to having gynecological exams from an early age.

Among the publications with broader reach identified by the survey, one of the first to cut a quote from Lula’s speech was posted at 11.59 p.m. on September 28 by Pâm, an influencer, founder of a Bolsonarista site called The Incorrupt, and member of Estúdio 5, a pro-Bolsonaro content-making hub aligned with Catholicism.
A user identified as Pâm posted: ‘Lula saying women ‘learn to be touched ever since they are little’ WHAT THE FUCK, PRESIDENT?
Are you NUTS???.
Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use.
At 12.28 a.m. on September 29, the Space Liberdade account published another cut from the same quote.
It took only a minute for the interpretation to be turned into an explicit accusation.
At 12.29 a.m., two other posts were already calling the president “a pedophile”; one of them requesting users to pass this claim along.
In the following hours, several users started acting to amplify the reach of the accusation.
Posts asked people to download and repost the video, suggested boosting the hashtag #LULAPEDOPHILE, and included messages like “it has to go viral.
At 2.48 a.m., a profile proposed to pick out two sentences from Lula’s speech, create a hashtag, and mobilize 10 to 20 influencers around it.
An account called Space Liberdade posted: ‘URGENT — Lula says men don’t like ‘to be touched’ and states that women learn ‘to be touched’ since they are little.
(…) a man doesn’t; he doesn’t know that once he has prostate cancer they will touch him a lot.
Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use.

Five hours before Pâm’s publication, users connected to the so-called “bolha da resenha” (hangout banter bubble) were already experimenting with Grok, forcing the tool to associate Lula with pedophilia.

The term describes an ecosystem of profiles, most of them anonymous, that combine aggressive humour, extremist political content, and reproducing chans aesthetics — anonymous forums well known as one of the main cradles of the current far-right.

items.title: Peru’s Indigenous people in Cutivireni and Oviri take the front line against Amazon wildfires

s: Indigenous guardians play a critical role in protecting the land, their homes, and their livelihoods

The Cool Earth initiative in Cutivireni and Oviri works around three key concepts: the monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the introduction of a flag-based system regarding safe times to conduct traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small blazes and prevent them from causing devastation to the Indigenous people in the rainforest.
Photo by Cool Earth, 2026; used with permission.
It’s September and 2026 has already been defined by wildfires spanning across the globe.
Driven by the heat and dryness of the climate crisis, outbursts on the edge of Bordeaux, France have forced 200,000 from their homes and led to deaths in Spain.
Smoke has billowed across the Canada-U.S. border, covering cities in smog.

Fires are expected to continue as seasons transition in the Southern Hemisphere, with a severe El Niño phenomenon that the United Nations warns will add pressure to an already scorching globe, risking similar conditions to those that — back in 2024 — drove the worst Amazonian wildfires in two decades.

With fire and drought risks set to increase in the coming months, Indigenous people in the Amazon rainforest are stepping up to take on new roles as fire brigade members, protecting both their homes and a key natural resource in the fight against climate change.

Ahead of this year’s El Niño weather pattern, Indigenous people from Peru’s Cutivireni and Oviri communities approached Cool Earth: they wanted to ensure they were equipped to fight any fires this coming season.

The organization’s long-established relationship with the two Indigenous groups and experience working with the Central Asháninka of the Ene River to create the Paamari programme, made it easier to establish four fire crews across communities that were already springing into action.
In Cutivireni, the newly formed Chullachaqui fire crew have faced multiple blazes.
Named after an Amazonian forest spirit, the crew understand the critical role they play in protecting the land, their homes, and their livelihoods.

In early August came one of the first tests of their training: alerted by people in the Tsyapo and Pajonal communities, community brigade members joined up with their partners in Central Cutivireni to tackle the fire, which they successfully put out.

Julio Acosta, Cool Earth’s Forest Data Manager, said that the organization really admires and appreciates how the communities have been making the best use of what they have been building with them, adding, “This early action taken in Tsyapo and Pajonal demonstrates how effectively they put into practice what they’ve learned in the workshops.”
The training was taken directly from concepts in the Paamari programme.

Similar to Paamari, the Cool Earth initiative with Cutivireni and Oviri works around three key concepts: the increased monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the introduction of a flag-based system regarding safe times to conduct traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small blazes and prevent them from causing devastation to the Indigenous people in the rainforest.
The communities themselves often act as the brigade’s eyes, alerting them to smoke or flames.

Working in close coordination with local authorities, brigade members first assess the wildfires and try to tame the blazes in their initial stage, before they require a more complex response by the authorities.
Acosta stressed the importance of highlighting the fact that the main work of these brigades lies in prevention, rather than initial response.
“This tends to be less visible,” he explained, {but the measures they take, such as the flag system, help reduce the occurrence of these fires.
Seeing the initiative and eagerness to learn more from the brigade members motivates us to expand and improve the work we’ve been implementing together.”

items.title: Hong Kong police launch AI-powered national security platform for school pupils

s: ‘May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils…’
Hong Kong police launch an AI-powered national security education platform for the city’s pupils during a ceremony on October 6, 2026.
Photo: HKPF, via Facebook.
Used with permission.
Hong Kong police have launched an artificial intelligence-powered national security education platform for young students.

The NSmarties AI Interactive Platform was officially launched on October 6, 2026, at a ceremony at Precious Blood Primary School in Ap Lei Chau, with about 700 pupils attending, police said in a Facebook post:

【 NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台 • 正式啟動 】 國家安全，由童心出發！ 由警務處國家安全處主辦的「NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台」今日（6日）於海怡寶血小學正式啟動！ 警務處處長周一鳴、警務處副處長（國家安全）江學禮、寶血會總會長區綺雯修女等一眾嘉賓，聯同約700位同學一同見證這個重要時刻。 啟動禮圓滿結束，標誌着國安教育以創新科技走進校園的新里程！ 願國安種子在同學心裏生根發芽，茁壯成長！
[ NSmarties: Children’s Hearts Protect Hong Kong AI Interactive Platform • Officially Launched ] National security begins with the hearts of children!

Organized by the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force, the ‘NSmarties: Children’s Hearts Protect Hong Kong AI Interactive Platform’ was officially launched today (6th) at Sea View Precious Blood Primary School!

Distinguished guests, including Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming, Deputy Commissioner of Police (National Security) Kelvin Kong Hok-lai, and Sister Au Yee-man, President of the Precious Blood Society, joined some 700 pupils in witnessing this momentous occasion.
The successful launch ceremony marks a new milestone in bringing national security education into schools through innovative technology!
May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils, and grow strong!

The platform, jointly developed by police and Hong Kong Qianfan Technology, lets students generate personalized stories centered on China’s “holistic approach to national security” — a framework pushed by Chinese President Xi Jinping that covers areas from politics and the economy to ecology and technology.
It also features the voices of Chow and security chief Chris Tang, who explain the city’s national security laws and security information.
The ceremony marked a “milestone” in bringing national security education into the city’s schools through innovative technologies, police said.
The NSmarties platform was first unveiled on National Security Education Day in April, but it was not fully launched to the public at that time.
Hong Kong has strengthened national security education alongside a crackdown since Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020 following the 2019 protests and unrest.
Beijing inserted national security legislation directly into Hong Kong’s mini-constitution in June 2020 following a year of pro-democracy protests and unrest.
It criminalized subversion, secession, collusion with foreign forces and terrorist acts — broadly defined to include disruption to transport and other infrastructure.
The move gave police sweeping new powers and led to hundreds of arrests amid new legal precedents, while dozens of civil society groups disappeared.
The authorities say it restored stability and peace to the city, rejecting criticism from trade partners, the UN and NGOs.

items.title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta

s: The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity
Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022.
Photo by Bjoertvedt.
Source: Wikipedia.
CC BY-SA 4.0
The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar.
If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.
Telenor operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022 with 18 million subscribers.
After the February 2021 coup, Telenor faced pressure after the junta demanded compliance with its surveillance and content blocking directives.
Telenor decided to leave Myanmar, but civil society groups raised strong objections that its local operations would be sold to a company with links to the junta.
In December 2024, activist group Justice For Myanmar filed a complaint against Telenor in Norway for breach of the Sanctions Act.
Norway rejected it, but the complaint was refiled in October 2025 with an additional charge of aiding and abetting crimes against humanity.
The Norwegian state has a 54-percent stake in Telenor.
In December 2025, the Norwegian Parliament initiated an investigation into the operations of Telenor in Myanmar.

The leader of the disciplinary committee of the Parliament said: “We must uncover how a state-owned company could cooperate with a brutal military regime (by handing over) customer information about the opposition [in Myanmar].”
In April 2026, a civil class action lawsuit was filed against Telenor in Norway by Myanmar citizens for sharing their sensitive personal data with the junta.
The complaint alleged that Telenor shared at least 1,253 phone numbers with the regime.
The data also included call logs and location data, names, addresses, ID numbers, Facebook, and bank accounts linked to mobile numbers.
Among the complainants is Tha Zin, the widow of rapper and lawmaker Phyo Zeya Thaw, who was arrested based on a trumped-up charge, convicted, and later executed by the junta.
Tha Zin said her husband was arrested right after his account information was accessed by the junta.
I lost my husband.
It is not just a wife losing her husband.
It is also a loss to the movement.
It is also a loss to democracy because my husband was committed to democracy and a youth leader.
Losing him means a loss to the country.
Lawyer Jan Magne Langseth summed up the content of the complaint.
Telenor ASA in Norway clearly contributed to the practice of handing over user data, despite the inherent risks for its customers in Myanmar.
We have evidence of cases where the team at HQ expressly recommended the data to be handed over.
In September 2026, Norway’s National Criminal Investigation Service and the interior security service searched the office of Telenor related to the charges filed against the company.
Justice for Myanmar spokesperson Yadanar Maung welcomed the decision of Norway authorities to investigate Telenor.
Telenor’s transfer of spyware to a military-linked company and sharing of sensitive data with the military junta was extensively documented
We hope this will finally lead to accountability for the harms Telenor has caused Myanmar people through its conduct and its dangerous divestment.
In several statements sent to the media, Telenor said it is cooperating with authorities with regard to the ongoing investigation.
It added that it needed to defend its employees in Myanmar.
In Myanmar, refusing requests from the military authorities could, in the worst case, have led to imprisonment, torture or the death penalty.
Telenor Myanmar had no real options.
We could not play Russian roulette with the lives of our employees.
Telenor media relations director David Fidjeland reiterated the same point.
Our employees risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty if the military authorities’ orders were not complied with.
We found that we had no real choice and that we could not put our employees’ lives at risk.

items.title: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance

s: The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest
Moscow subway cameras are connected to a facial recognition system.
Screenshot taken from the YouTube video “Facial recognition cameras help detain dissidents in the Moscow metro” by the DW YouTube channel; fair use.
Sonya, from Stavropol Krai, Russia, is 15 years old.
In June 2026, she was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor, connected to a February 2026 incident in which she had written the surname “Navalny” on a bus stop.
That stop happened to be in a district that was being monitored by officers from the Center for Combating Extremism, commonly called Center E.
Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan who was also identified from surveillance footage, was given three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” in red marker on buildings.
Authoritarian regimes are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) as a technology of political survival.

Cameras with facial recognition, video analytics, biometric databases, digital IDs, social media monitoring, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) systems, and public service platforms are gradually merging into a single infrastructure of control.
Such a system makes it possible not only to observe citizens in real time, but also to reconstruct their past movements, connections, habits, communications, and political activity.

The main risk is that AI and related technologies make repression faster and less visible: the state no longer needs to constantly demonstrate force if citizens know they can be identified retroactively.
Modern digital authoritarianism is not developing in isolation, but through the international exchange of technologies, standards, and practices.

China, Russia, Iran, Belarus, Venezuela, countries in Africa, Western and Central Asia, and companies connected to them, sell and exchange AI infrastructure tools that are being used for the purpose of repression.
Western technologies a re also being bought and exchanged within authoritarian regimes.

In early June 2026, Sberbank Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin told Reuters that the company was offering countries in the Global South access to Russian AI models that would take “local values” into account.
Vedyakhin was referring to specific large language models (LLMs) — GigaChat and YandexGPT — which Russia had been trying to develop since 2019.
However, as IT expert Alexander Isavnin told journalists at the podcast Zhivoy Gvozd, Russian generative AI models lag behind American and Chinese models and cannot even generate text in Cyrillic.

Yet, new national and sovereign AI models are supposed to reflect traditional values, including patriotism, service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate, a strong family, historical memory and continuity between generations, and unity of the peoples of Russia.
These models are expected to be trained on domestic, authentically Russian material.

It is reasonable to assume that in countries like those in Western Asia, Russian AI models will reflect adherence to Islamic traditions, while in Argentina, perhaps, they will reflect respect for football from an early age.

Developers, meanwhile, do not understand how people with no idea about how any of this works can write AI laws: “In places, the document reads as if it was written by people who had only ever seen LLMs in local news.
From the perspective of global democracy, however, this illiteracy among Russian lawmakers suggests that Russia is unlikely to supply LLMs to autocracies around the world.
China, by contrast — unlike American developers — makes its language models open in principle, meaning that anyone can take the code and modify it for their own needs.

In China, all LLMs are controlled and tightly regulated by the state, so party censorship is written into the code from the start — for example, you cannot get an answer about the Tiananmen Square protests.
However, the models are distributed as open source, which is why more than 50 percent of Chinese model users come from developers, including those in the Global South.

items.title: In Kyrgyzstan, persons with disabilities are collecting proof of physical barriers to hold the government accountable

s: Physical barriers are being exposed by those who are affected the most
Participants of the Oasis Data Lab workshop in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
Image by the public fund Oasis.
Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Kyrgyzstan’s progress in creating an inclusive and accessible environment for people with disabilities remains limited after seven years of ratifying the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019.

Despite a legal responsibility to undertake measures that would remove legal and physical barriers and help people with disabilities lead independent social and economic lives, the government has not prioritized this commitment at the level requested by the country’s disabled community.

In such circumstances, holding the government accountable requires proof of how much physical infrastructure remains inaccessible for the more than 218,000 people with disabilities in the country — about three percent of the population.

One of the organizations leading this effort in Kyrgyzstan is the public fund “Oasis”, which is documenting the level of physical inaccessibility in the capital, Bishkek, with the help of people with disabilities who are auditing objects through their real-life experiences.
Global Voices conducted a written interview with Oasis to learn about this work, which is being carried out under the Digital Sparks project.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.
Oasis (O): Founded in 2003, Oasis is a Kyrgyz civil society organization working to build inclusive communities where everyone can participate and reach their full potential.
We joined the project because we know that it is not possible to build an inclusive city without listening to the people navigating its barriers every day.
In Bishkek, we saw accessibility discussed through policies and assumptions, while lived experiences remained largely invisible.
We wanted to change that to make exclusion visible, measurable, and impossible to overlook with the help of data.
Digital Sparks helped us build the Oasis Data Lab, bringing together citizen-generated data, digital mapping, storytelling, and advocacy.
Our goal was not simply to create a map, but to build a bridge between lived experience and public decision-making, turning everyday barriers into evidence for change.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
O: The project grew from a practical problem: people with disabilities face barriers across Bishkek, but these barriers were not being systematically documented.
Public transport, entrances, ramps, toilets, signage, and other parts of the urban environment can make everyday participation difficult.
Yet without reliable and regularly updated data, these problems remain easy to overlook.
Kyrgyzstan ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019, but there is still a gap between formal commitments and everyday accessibility.
Previous assessments were limited and did not create a living public record that could be used to monitor progress.
We therefore started from a simple principle: before accessibility can be improved, it has to be measured.
And the people who experience these barriers every day should be directly involved in producing that evidence.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
O: Through Digital Sparks, we developed Oasis Data Lab into a more structured space for digital civic participation.
We brought together more than 30 young people, including people with physical disabilities, blind and low-vision participants, deaf participants, social activists, and urban experts.

items.title: Poetry book promotes Chabacano, Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language

s: A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language.
The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers.
Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop.
In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano, a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga.
Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology.
This led to the launch of the “ Sombra y Luz ” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors.
The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity.

Herrera said, “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”
He added that the book title aims to convey a message of contrast about the changes in Zamboanga City.
The book cover also provides a nostalgic reference to the flowers that decorated the city in the past.
The cover features an American-era style lamppost that can be seen along the Zamboanga boulevard.
The cover also features bougainvilleas which my dad tells me were ubiquitous in Zamboanga City back when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores.
Herrera’s poem in the anthology mentions flowers and birds that enrich life in the city.
Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit! Twit! Twit!
Entero el dia.
Mio pueblo Ciudad de Zamboanga, Ciudad de Flores que llama.
De noche mucho pajaro ay columbra, Na maga cable de corriente ta esta.
Birds that fly and flutter freely, Perched upon the branches of trees, Singing and calling each other joyfully, Tweet! Tweet! Tweet!
All day long.
Oh, my beloved City of Zamboanga, City of Flowers, they call you.
At night, many birds can be found, Sitting on wires, that’s what they do.
In an interview with Global Voices, Herrera noted the heavy use of Spanish words in the selected poems:
…there is a lot of debate with regards to what Chabacano poetry should look like.
For some, they like it with a lot of Spanish words and for others, they like it to be exactly as how Chabacano appears in everyday conversations.
Most of the poems submitted leaned heavily on Spanish words, I think primarily because Chabacano writers rely on Spanish words to make their works sound more formal as well as more poetic.
Since it’s poetry, I thought that it was alright to present Chabacano in an idealistic manner.
He added that the anthology seeks to encourage more people to accept the various ways that Chabacano is used.
For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box.
I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano.
This approach is evident in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which celebrates Chabacano as a living language.

Through references to poems, essays, fables, and the stories passed down by elders, the author reminds readers that the language continues to thrive when it is written, spoken, and shared with others.
The title itself is noteworthy for its use of both Chavacano and Chabacano, reflecting the coexistence of two accepted spellings of the language.
In doing so, the poem highlights not only the importance of preserving Chabacano, but also the richness and diversity of its written tradition.
Herrera’s interview with Asymptote Journal noted the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, and his hope that the book project can lead to more literary initiatives.

items.title: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan

s: Nepali communities live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities
Settlements across the Tadi River, Devighat in Nuwakot District.
Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026.
Used with permission.

Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood, which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026.
This latest disaster has added to the wounds of communities who live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities.

The climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has devastated a once-popular tourist landscape, destroying its natural beauty and economic opportunities, with settlements heartbreakingly reduced to rubble and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges and hydro-power facilities, washed away.
The full death toll remains officially unconfirmed.
Survivors still come to search for their belongings in Devighatm, Nuwakot District.
Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026.
Used with permission.
But an uncomfortable truth lies behind the devastation: The human cost of such disasters often goes ignored.
Behind the statistics are stories of broken dreams, lost livelihoods, buried memories.
There are families trying to stay alive without their loved ones, communities faced with an uncertain future, and countless people trying to make lives reconnect and rebuild from what little is left.
The task of rebuilding is huge.
The damage is not only to homes, roads and bridges, but also to farms and local businesses.
Kyodo News reports via AP that 7,500 homes were damaged or completely destroyed, with costs of recovery hitting USD 4.77 billion.
The government has now moved from emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction and has also acknowledged the risks posed by possible glacial outburst floods ( GLOFs ) and other hazards.
The destruction of bridges and transport links has made surviving communities vulnerable and slowed reconstruction, exposing residents to further risk.
Buildings left standing, and homes left empty in the Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District.
Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026.
Used with permission.
To this end, joint efforts are underway to rebuild damaged infrastructure and restore vital services.
But pledged assistance is not the same as money that has actually been received and delivered to affected communities.
Nepal’s Ministry of Finance’s foreign assistance tracker shows that Nepal has received USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds.
Such tracking can help bring transparency to the collection and distribution of aid.
The Prime Minister's Office separately reported that USD 50.47 million of assistance (cash, materials, and teams) had been pledged.
No formal update has been given on the implementation of longer-term reconstruction plans.
Most of the aid is still going to meet immediate needs like medical aid, food, and temporary shelters, such as tents.
What are houses without their people called?
Photo featuring reporter Susmita Aryal.
Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Maya Devi Aryal on October 7, 2026.
Used with permission.
Many affected communities remain far from rebuilt infrastructure and restored livelihoods.
India, China, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are providing assistance, and the Asian Development Bank and other international financial institutions have committed funds.
Yet recovery is likely to progress unevenly.
The challenge for affected communities is not just to rebuild what was lost but to restore livelihoods, public services and a sense of security in the face of recurring environmental hazards.
In the following photo essay, Global Voices highlights how Nepali citizens are still affected by the disaster.
All photos were taken by Susmita Aryal in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot District on October 7, 2026.
Tara Devi Tamang and others waiting for relief and basic needs provided at the Bidur Municipality Office, Nuwakot District.
Image via Susmita Aryal.
Used with permission
Daily essentials scattered around the community in Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District.
Image via Susmita Aryal.
Used with permission.

items.title: What African elections can learn from the Borana Gadaa system

s: Can the Borana Gadaa system inspire fairer elections, peaceful transitions, and stronger democracy across Africa?
A Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony held by the Borana Oromo people in Southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya.
They have long practiced rotational, peaceful leadership transfer, known as the Borana Gadaa system.
Photo used with permission.
This article by Diba Kosi Bilinga was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026.
An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.
Every election season, much of Africa braces itself.
In some cases, incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets.
The pattern repeats: disputed results, ethnic mobilization, coups, or leaders who refuse to leave.
Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the Borana Oromo people have long practiced rotational, peacefully transferred leadership.
Known as the Borana Gadaa system, UNESCO inscribed it in 2016 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life, resolves conflict, and protects women’s rights.

This article asks a question: What can African leaders, electoral commissions, political parties, and citizens learn from a governance model that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups, without third-term referenda, and without the bloodshed that so often accompanies modern African elections?
Borana leadership rotates on a fixed eight-year cycle among five Gogeessas (parties).
Each governs for one Gadaa period, then hands over power, returning to the first after 40 years — a rotation built into the structure itself.
Compare this to Africa’s modern pattern.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) director Ida Sawyer describes a “constitutional coup” pattern: leaders who cannot win re-election simply rewrite the laws to get their way.

Cameroon’s Paul Biya erased term limits in 2008 and has ruled since 1982; Uganda’s Museveni scrapped his in 2005; Rwanda, Burundi, Togo, Djibouti, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have each amended their constitutions to extend a president’s tenure.
Gadaa’s lesson is structural: When a time limit is built into the system itself, rather than a leader’s promise, departure never has to be settled by force.
Gadaa systems treat leadership as something built over decades, not switched on by an election.

Members pass through age-grades from childhood, absorbing law, custom, and ritual responsibility long before they are eligible to lead — knowledge oral historians formally transmit across generations.
Most African political systems do the opposite: Candidates are selected first, and asked whether they are fit to govern only afterward.
Patronage, money, and ethnic arithmetic often outweigh demonstrated understanding of law or public finance, producing leaders who improvise governance while learning on the job.

The lesson for African parties and civic institutions: Build structured pipelines — in local councils, youth wings, and civil service — that expose future leaders to responsibility long before a national mandate.
Under the Gadaa system, at the Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony, authority passes from the outgoing ruling class to the incoming one, understood by the whole community as final and binding.
Every eight years, the Gumi Gaayo assembly, held under the sacred Odaa tree, reviews the era’s laws and blesses the incoming leadership.
Contrast that with Kenya’s 2007 to 08 crisis, when a disputed result triggered ethnic violence that killed roughly 1,000 people and displaced 500,000, per HRW’s investigation.
Ivory Coast saw a similar rupture in 2010 to 2011, leading to a civil war.
In the Borana Gadaa system, succession is scripted years in advance.
In much of Africa, it is an open question resolved only after votes are contested.

items.title: When free speech has a price: Youth voices in Mozambique

s: When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence
A group of men during a peaceful protest; one of them holds a microphone and a banner.
Photo taken by Stephanie Douglas. Nigeria. Via Pexels.
Pexels License.

In Mozambique, freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014, a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique.

However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience.
In music, for example, this contradiction is clear.
Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo.

More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s, but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party.
Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces.
Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “ O ciclo da Censura ” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?
This is not just a provocative artistic comment.
It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences.
Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically.

While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum, digital platforms for monitoring local governance, cultural associations, and artistic initiatives.
This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces.
However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order.
One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools.
The measure was presented as a response to sexual harassment, but it implied that female students’ clothing choices were the cause of the harm they suffered.

By holding the girls accountable instead of the aggressors, the debate revealed something deeper: the dispute over control of the female body and the right of young women to define their own identity.
During the demonstrations, the Spanish activist Eva Anadón Moreno was detained and subsequently expelled from Mozambique for participating in the protest.
In recent years, censorship in Mozambique has rarely come in the form of explicit prohibitions.
However, that does not mean that fear and self-censorship are entirely absent.
In a 2010 interview, Azagaia observed that the biggest obstacle to freedom of expression in Mozambique was not necessarily direct police intimidation, but rather economic precarity.
When many job opportunities depend, directly or indirectly, on relationships with established power structures, public criticism can put people at risk.
This results in what could be called the “economy of silence.
Journalists avoid certain topics, artists moderate what they say, public officials keep their opinions quiet, and young activists learn that words can carry a high cost.
Freedom then ceases to be merely a legal issue and becomes a matter of survival.
In this context, protest music takes on a particular political value.
It breaks the collective silence and develops communities of recognition-building, where experiences of injustice find language, memory, and solidarity.

items.title: Bangladesh-Malaysia recruitment reforms revive old questions over the cost of migration

s: Repeated disruptions raise concerns over recruitment transparency and migrant workers’ protection from exploitation.

On Saturday, October 5, 2024, a Memorandum of Collaboration (MOC) was signed in Dhaka between the Wage Earners Welfare Board and Malaysia's PERKESO, regarding the expansion of the labor market in Malaysia.
Image via Wikipedia by Press Information Department of Bangladesh.
Public Domain.

Officials in both Bangladesh and Malaysia’s have made repeated attempts to reform the countries’ labour migration relationship, leading to numerous suspensions and reopenings over more than three decades.

Howeverm, on August 30, 2026, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, Mir Shahe Alam, announced that Malaysia would recruit around 200,000 Bangladeshi workers over six months, with departures expected to begin in late September.
He also referred to a plan to send 10,000 workers without requiring them to bear migration costs.
Two days later, however, Malaysia’s government spokesperson Fahmi Fadzil clarified that the figure of 200,000 workers did not represent an official government position.
The clarification introduced fresh uncertainty over the scale and timing of the recruitment drive.
The mixed signals came as the two countries were trying to reset a labour migration corridor that has faced repeated allegations of excessive recruitment fees, syndication and worker exploitation.

Bangladesh first entered into an agreement with Malaysia for the systematic transfer of labour in 1992, followed by another agreement in 1994 that provided for the recruitment of 50,000 workers annually, mainly for the construction sector.
Between 1992 and 1998, around 307,000 Bangladeshi workers were issued permits to work in Malaysia.
But recruitment was halted in 1997 amid a rise in unauthorised migration.
During that period, local brokers could charge workers between USD 2,000 (approximately BDT 245,700) and USD 3,000 (approximately BDT 368,600) for authorised migration.
In an effort to reduce recruitment malpractice and costs, the two governments turned to a government-to-government model ( G2G model ) in 2012.
The programme initially aimed to recruit around 30,000 Bangladeshi workers for Malaysia’s palm-oil sector.
More than 1.4 million people registered and workers were selected through a lottery system.
The G2G arrangement substantially reduced migration costs, but it struggled to meet its recruitment targets.
The system was later replaced by the G2G Plus arrangement.
Under the model introduced in 2016, Malaysia selected only 10 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies.

Although the agreed migration cost was around BDT 37,000-40,000 (approximately USD 300 to USD 325), later reports put the amount actually paid by workers at an average of around BDT 300,000 to 400,000 (approximately USD 2,450 to USD 3,260).
Allegations of syndication, high costs and other irregularities eventually led Malaysia to suspend recruitment again in 2018.
Recruitment resumed following a new memorandum of understanding signed in December 2021.
Between 2022 and 2024, 476,672 Bangladeshi workers were sent to Malaysia through 101 recruiting agencies.
But by June 2024, the labour market had again closed to new Bangladeshi recruits amid concerns over high migration costs and worker exploitation.

Against this history of repeated closed and reopened borders, the latest attempt to reset recruitment has revived a familiar question: whether the new arrangement can reduce the financial burden on workers and prevent the problems that undermined earlier recruitment systems.
On August 28, 2026, Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment outlined a broader recruitment arrangement involving 338 entities.
Malaysia had directly selected 25 recruiting agencies, while 312 others were approved to work as associates.
The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited, or BOESL, was also included.
Under the same arrangement, Malaysia had agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers on a zero-cost basis.
Prospective migrants were also warned not to make payments, undergo medical examinations or hand over their passports until formal instructions were issued.
That warning stands out against the record of the previous recruitment cycle.

items.title: Trump’s ‘Agreements on Reciprocal Trade’ (ARTs) threaten equitable access to the internet in Global South

s: The provision could give the U.S. the power to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers in signatory countries

This article, written by Prapasiri “Nan” Suttisome, was first published by EngageMedia, a non-profit media, technology, and culture organization, and an edited version is republished here as part of a content-sharing agreement.
It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism.
You can support this coverage by donating here.
Around the world, one in every three people has no reliable access to the internet.
Unequal access to the internet creates digital divides that can limit civic participation, undermine access to education and healthcare, and deepen inequality.
It can also reduce innovation, industrial growth, and economic output.
Reducing digital divides is recognized as essential for progress on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals, as reaffirmed by the more recent Global Digital Compact, 2024.
However, this goal could be threatened by the controversial reciprocal trade agreements (ARTs) signed by the U.S. since February 2025.

To date, the U.S. has signed ARTs with 10 countries — Malaysia, Cambodia, El Salvador, Argentina, Ecuador, Guatemala, Bangladesh, Taiwan, Jordan, and Indonesia — with framework deals in place with several others.

Hidden in most of these deals is a provision that requires these countries to refrain from using information and communication technology (ICT) suppliers that may “compromise the security, safeguards, and intellectual property of ICT infrastructure, including 5G, 6G, communication satellites, and undersea cables.
The ARTs with El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, and Malaysia further require them to consult with the U.S. on which suppliers meet these standards.
The purpose of this provision is, simply put, to give the U.S. the ability to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers such as Huawei and ZTE from these countries, should it so choose.
This could also benefit U.S. suppliers such as CISCO and Hewlett Packard, amongst others.

This provision therefore gives the U.S. a great deal of power, which, if misused, could significantly limit network rollout and development in the signatory countries, adversely affecting digital connectivity, increasing digital divides, and reducing economic growth.
This is significant, as most of the countries that have signed up to ARTs are low-income nations with significant digital divides.
For example, internet penetration in Bangladesh, El Salvador, Indonesia, Guatemala, and Cambodia is 53.4 percent, 66.5 percent, 72.8 percent, 60.2 percent, and 68.5 percent, respectively.
This has major implications for the connectivity of essential public infrastructure, especially in rural communities.
For instance, over 100,000 schools lack internet connectivity in Indonesia, while approximately 12 percent of schools lack access to the internet in Guatemala.
Cambodia fares worse, with only about 22 percent of schools having functional computers, let alone internet access.
A primary reason for the persistence of digital divides is the absence of necessary ICT infrastructure.
The International Telecommunication Union has estimated a USD 1.6 trillion investment gap in ICT infrastructure by 2030.

In many parts of the developing world, China has filled the ICT infrastructure investment gap, including through soft loans provided through the Digital Silk Road (DSR), part of the Belt and Road Initiative.
These loans are often provided at below-market rates and tied to the use of Chinese ICT suppliers.
The scale of funding provided under the DSR is huge.
For example, Chinese ICT infrastructure financing across Africa as far back as 2017 dwarfed the combined funds from African governments, multilateral agencies, and G7 nations.

Developing countries are caught between a rock and a hard place as it’s increasingly clear that foreign financial aid and investment —whether from China or the West — rarely comes without strings attached.

items.title: How Ecuador is fighting to keep industrial trans fats off the food shelf

s: A public health battle over what ends up on Ecuador’s food shelves
Civil society, academia, and the State met in Quito to discuss progress toward the regulation of trans fatty acids in a country where non-communicable diseases account for more than 76% of deaths.
Photo by Salomé Rosales Estrella/Minga por la Pachamama, 2026.
Used with permission.
“What are we eating?
Foods that regenerate or products that degenerate life?” asked Eliana Estrella on September 7, 2026, in the auditorium of Universidad San Francisco de Quito in Ecuador.

The popular communicator and member of the Committee of Users of the Food Market (CUUM) was speaking at the Hearts Free of Trans Fats meeting, before social organizations, academia and health agencies.
The event was the first activity in a packed three-day agenda.

On September 8, civic organizations and representatives of academia met at FLACSO Ecuador for the workshop “Adding Voices for Health: Ecuador Meeting 2026,” dedicated to identifying priorities, capacities and advocacy strategies regarding noncommunicable diseases, while on September 10, the discussion “Food for Life” examined the responses promoted by civil society, their difficulties and their challenges.
Estrella’s question brought the discussion back to an everyday scene: a person standing in front of a shelf.

Products like margarines, cookies, spreads, doughnuts, cakes and some fried foods may contain industrial trans fats, and depend on the oils, fats and processes used to make them — a difference that is not always evident when making a choice.
The World Health Organization (WHO) explains that these fats are produced mainly through partial hydrogenation: hydrogen is added to a liquid oil to make it solid or semi-solid.
This creates partially hydrogenated oils, used in certain foods to modify their texture and extend their shelf life — an advantage for manufacturing and preservation, but not for health.
Natural trans fats also exist in the meat and dairy products of ruminants.
The WHO considers both to be harmful, but regulatory efforts focus on industrial trans fats because they can be eliminated from the food supply and replaced with healthier fats and oils.

Beatriz Champagne, executive director of Coalición América Saludable (CLAS), a regional collective that brings together more than 200 organizations and individuals, placed the problem beyond individual decisions: “They are not diseases of chance; they are the predictable result of health systems, food systems and regulatory processes that still do not protect the population.”

The WHO estimates that each year, more than 278,000 deaths are attributable to the consumption of industrial trans fats, which is associated with a higher risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and death.

Daniel Antiporta, the Pan American Health Organization’s (PAHO) representative at the meeting, addressed the regional scope of the problem: more than 150,000 deaths in the Americas, nearly half of them premature.
The impact, he warned, is not limited to years of productivity lost; it also compromises well-being and human development.
Estrella, meanwhile, focused on the conditions surrounding each purchase.

Describing these products as “accessible,” “cheap,” and promoted through major marketing investments, she argued that they displace fresh foods and local agriculture, because consumers’ money stops reaching the people who produce them.
Malek Batal, a professor at the University of Montreal’s Department of Nutrition, linked those decisions to the available supply: “We can only buy what exists and what exists at an affordable price.
Focusing recommendations exclusively on individuals, he added, can increase frustration and the feeling of being unable to care for one’s own health.
In subsequent interviews for this article, Champagne and Estrella explained how the problem cuts across everyday life.
Champagne noted that while hydrogenation made it possible to produce solid fats and extend the shelf life of some products, what facilitates preservation can leave consequences that last much longer.
A heart attack, for example, may require emergency care, medication and surgery; a stroke can affect speech or movement, and make permanent care necessary.

items.title: Subsea cables and oil pipelines: The infrastructure linking AI, empire, and occupation

s: Internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making
The internet has always been illusive.
Stretching bodies of water, screens, and time zones, it exists in a plurality increasingly shaped by big tech.
And the cables mediate this; the cables are its nervous system.

With over 600 active and planned underwater internet cables spanning over 1.5 million kilometers around the globe, the majority of subsea infrastructure is predominantly owned and operated by US tech monopolies, namely Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft.
This infrastructure is largely laid on trans-Atlantic slave ship and oil extraction routes, algorithmically bound by a legacy of colonial violence and exploitative labor practices.

Three years after the internet was made accessible to the public, the US government passed the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which incentivized independent companies and communications services to compete in the global market.

Relaxed regulations and an end to the cap on radio station ownership created more opportunities for media conglomerates — the majority of which are funded by private tech companies — to own, operate, and influence public-facing content.
This is still true today, as Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft currently own roughly over 75 percent of subsea cables around the world.
These companies control where information physically flows and the platforms through which this information, this data, circulates.

The growing importance of subsea cables in military and economic policy for major world powers like the US, Israel, and Saudi Arabia offers an entry point into understanding the corrosive, yet dependent, relationship between AI and oil infrastructure.

Earlier this year, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced the Communications and Technology Transparency Act as an update to the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, expanding the “malicious technology and equipment from foreign adversaries” on the FCC’s control list to include China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran.

This comes in response to Iran restricting access through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial point for global oil shipping and subsea cable infrastructure in which the US has invested a significant amount.

We have not seen this kind of surge in subsea cable investment since the internet went public in 1993, effectively shifting the digital sphere from a privatized space for military communications into a public playground.

Around this time, companies like Amazon and eBay came online alongside chatrooms, search engines, independent news outlets, and, in turn, the digital sphere entered the homes of those who could afford it.
Today, internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making.

China has supposedly asked Iran to help defend against Houthi attacks along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as Saudi Aramco oil exports, in which it has invested USD 4 billion, remain vulnerable.

Chinese and US-based companies Alibaba, Amazon, IBM, Google, and Microsoft maintain some of the largest investments in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) having the most data center and cloud projects.

This internet infrastructure is deeply tied to oil infrastructure, as the natural gas systems increasingly used to keep data centers in America running are optimized by AI, effectively pillaging the physical and digital platforms through which local communities connect and express themselves.
At the atomic level, crude oil is made almost entirely of hydrocarbons, which AI has been used to optimize in the form of wellbore drilling tools and environmental assessments.
In 2025, US President Donald Trump signed a $600 billion investment commitment in technological and defense systems with Saudi Arabia.

In the same month, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) launched HUMAIN, a vertically integrated AI company developing an Arabic-first language learning model, with full computing infrastructure located in Saudi Arabia.

items.title: Alibaba sues Pentagon to denounce being classified as a Chinese military affiliate

s: China’s big tech governance model looms over Alibaba’s lawsuit against the Pentagon
As the U.S.

Department of Defense expanded its Section 1260H list of “Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.” in June 2026, three dominant internet and technology giants — Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent (BAT) — have been flagged as an extension of the Chinese state and subject to the Pentagon procurement ban that excludes them from DoD’s supply chain.
The listing also signals an increasing risk of further sanctions from the Department of Commerce or the Treasury.
Alibaba protested the classification by suing the Pentagon.
In the court filing, Alibaba denied any affiliation with the Chinese military or any role in China’s state-directed military-civil fusion strategy.
It argued that the listing and ban “has no basis in fact or law” and deprives the company of future business opportunities.
It also argues that the abrupt announcement has violated the company’s constitutional right to explain its position.

Section 1260H was introduced in 2021 to address the so-called Chinese state strategy of “ military-civil fusion,” which facilitates the transfer of commercial tech companies’ technology or research to Chinese defense bases.

The DoD’s statement describes Alibaba as “indirectly affiliated with SASAC” ( State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council of the People’s Republic of China), and a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base” because it is affiliated with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT).

Setting aside the debate over procedural justice, the public records — mostly international and Chinese domestic news reports — that the DoD submitted to the court as evidence of its decision largely reflect the authoritative nature of China’s big-tech governance, highlighting Alibaba’s strategic alignment with the Chinese government’s censorship, technology, and military development strategy.

Citing news reports about China’s censorship and Alibaba’s official document about its milestone in tech development in its submission to the court, DoD suggests the company plays an active role in building China’s censorship regime.
Indeed, China has more than a dozen laws and regulations.
The Cybersecurity Law (2017), for example, requires network operators to monitor, halt, and delete prohibited content; preserve logs; and report incidents to government authorities.

Provisions on the Governance of Cyber Information Content Ecosystem (2020) classify content into three major categories: positive, illegal, and negative, and demand that operators promote, delete, and suppress them accordingly.
AI-related laws ban the use of algorithms to “influence public opinion” or encourage addiction/overconsumption, and ensure generative AI models adhere to the state’s “core socialist values.”

Alibaba argued that compliance with Chinese regulations should not be interpreted as evidence of military ties, since all multinational companies operating in China, including American firms, must follow local laws.

However, the Pentagon’s public record attachment to the court suggests that Alibaba not only adheres to the censorship requirements in its consumer platforms, generative AIs, and mobile browser, but also develops censorship technology such as Alibaba “Green AI,” which automates real-time filtering across text, images, voice, video, and streaming data, and sells the content moderation tools to both domestic and overseas developers, e-commerce vendors, video streaming services, and gaming platforms, so that they can operate within China’s legal requirements.

Beyond assisting and exporting censorship technology, which is not for military purposes, the DoD’s court filing also includes news reports and commentary about the disappearance of its founder, Jack Ma, in late November 2020.

Prior to Jack Ma’s disappearance, on October 24, 2020, he criticized China’s banking system as being outdated, and later, on November 3, Alibaba’s Ant Finance’s USD 37 billion dual listing in Shanghai and Hong Kong stock markets was suspended.
His disappearance coincided with the Chinese authorities’ antitrust investigation against Alibaba, which was eventually fined USD 2.75 billion for forcing merchants to choose between platforms.

items.title: El Niño speeds climate crisis and tests Latin America’s food security

s: As the climate pattern intensifies, Latin America faces a growing food security challenge
This article by Fabiola Chambi first appeared in CONNECTAS, in Spanish, on September 2, 2026.
An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.
“We are sad, completely desperate.
We have lost llamas, alpacas, sheep — we haven’t even been able to count them all yet […] That is how we make a living.
We put our children through school and sell our products in the city.
The last heavy snowfall René Luna could remember had caught him by surprise nearly 25 years ago, but never anything like this.
